title: Cap. VII: Resp. 3 — Apostolic wisdom, not prescribed formulas; Pelagius objection
pass_a_gloss: Resp. 3 — vix ferendum: si Paulus imputationem docere voluisset, debuisse potius ἐν ᾧ quam ἐφ᾽ ᾧ. Garissoles: Qui nos sumus Apostolo praescribere loquendi rationem/formulas? ἐν + ἐπί frequenter eundem sensum. Placeus clementer: autor rationis abhorret ab hujusmodi arrogantia; non praescribit sed a sapientia/prudentia Apostoli (summa) ducit argumentum. Quaerebatur: quid ἐφ᾽ ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον significare voluit? Aiunt: primum Adami peccatum actuale omnibus imputatum immediate. Mentem Apostolo tribuunt (non dicam praescribunt) + verba minus accommodata inflectunt (ἐπί pro ἐν, nulla ratione). Ille objicit: minus convenit sapientiae Apostolicae — doctrina ardua, a sensu communi abhorrens, alibi non in Scriptura → consentaneum aperte/diserte hic doceri. Si ἐν ᾧ dixisset: non opus enallage ἐπί→ἐν; minus ambigua ἐν ᾧ; ἐφ᾽ ᾧ rarius = eo quod/quatenus. Apostolus consulto ἐφ᾽ ᾧ maluit quam ἐν ᾧ; removerit + separaverit ἀνθρώπου pluribus interpositis; impediverit relativum ᾧ. Cur sine necessitate vim inferre verbis/collocationi vs retenta ἐφ᾽ ᾧ proprietate + Apostolico commatum situ admittere sententiam quam nemo non Pelagianus negare potest veram? Garissoles Pelagius/Socinus tu quoque: si Scriptura docere voluisset peccatum generatione / Christum Mediatorem merito+satisfactione → verbis claris. Placeus: sequaces possunt objicere; respondemus non 'nostrum non est Deo praescribere' (sophisticum cum Dei mens in quaestione) sed rem: non abhorret a conscientiae sensu + tam disertis verbis exprimitur ut nisi magna vis afferatur detorqueri nequeant.
pass_b_english: Response 3. It seems scarcely bearable that it is said: if Paul had wished to teach imputation, he ought rather to have said ἐν ᾧ than ἐφ᾽ ᾧ. For who are we who dare prescribe to the Apostle a manner of speaking and formulas — especially when ἐν and ἐπί so frequently have the same sense and signification? Gently, I ask: without doubt the author of that reason abhors vehemently from arrogance of this kind. He does not prescribe to the Apostle a manner of speaking and formulas; he draws an argument from his wisdom and prudence, which is established to have been the highest. It was asked what the Apostle wished to signify by the words ἐφ᾽ ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον (Romans 5:12). Some say he wished to signify that Adam's first actual sin was imputed to all men, and that immediately. Since therefore they attribute this mind to the Apostle — I will not say they prescribe it, but because it so pleases them — and toward that mind they bend a little his words, less accommodating as they are, affirming that ἐπί is put for ἐν with no reason given. He objects that this less befits Apostolic wisdom. For since a doctrine of this kind is very hard, and abhorrent from common sense, and is not taught elsewhere in Scripture, it was fitting that at least in this one place it be taught openly and in express words — or at least in those words which, though falsely, are nevertheless held as express by those who dissent from us in this cause. If at least he had said ἐν ᾧ, there would have been no need to recur to an enallage of the preposition ἐπί put for ἐν, and the signification of the words ἐν ᾧ would have been less ambiguous: for much more rarely than ἐφ᾽ ᾧ do they signify "in that," "inasmuch as," and so on. Since therefore the Apostle deliberately preferred to say ἐφ᾽ ᾧ rather than ἐν ᾧ, and as much as could be done removed them from those antecedents, and by several things interposed separated the noun ἀνθρώπου, and so hindered the relative ᾧ from being referred to it as antecedent — why without necessity, without reason, do we prefer to force some violence upon his words and upon the collocation of the words, so that they seem somehow to say what cannot be gathered from them, rather than, retaining the propriety of the words ἐφ᾽ ᾧ and the Apostolic situ of the clauses, admit that sense of his words which in itself no one but a Pelagian can deny to be true? But what, he says, will hinder Pelagius or Socinus from objecting by the same reason: if Scripture had wished to teach either that sin is propagated by generation, or that Christ is Mediator by merit and satisfaction, it would have expressed it, or ought to have expressed it, in clear and perspicuous words, since the matter is hard and not enough accommodated to the common sense of men? Altogether nothing will hinder the followers of Pelagius and Socinus from being able to object this if they wish; but nothing will hinder us either from answering those who object — not what D. Garissoles wants, that it is not ours to prescribe to God manners and modes of speaking (for this, when God's mind and sentence is turned in the question, can seem sophistic); but what the fact is: that it neither abhors in any way from the sense of conscience, and is expressed in Scripture in words so express and clear that, unless great force is brought upon them, they cannot be twisted into another sense.
source_text: Resp. 3. vix ferendum videri, quod dicitur, si Paulus imputationem docere voluisset, debuisse potius ἐν ᾧ dicere quam ἐφ᾽ ᾧ. Qui enim nos sumus, qui Apostolo praescribere audeamus loquendi rationem, et formulas, praesertim cum ἐν et ἐπί tam frequenter eundem sensum et significationem habeant? Clementer quaeso: abhorret enim sine dubio vehementer ab hujusmodi arrogantia rationis illius autor. Non praescribit Apostolo loquendi rationem et formulas, sed ab ejus sapientia et prudentia, quam summam fuisse constat, ducit argumentum. Quaerebatur quid Apostolus significare voluit verbis ἐφ᾽ ᾧ πάντες ἥμαρτον? Aiunt quidam eum significare voluisse, primum Adami peccatum actuale omnibus hominibus imputatum fuisse, et quidem immediate. Quoniam ergo hanc mentem Apostolo, non dicam praescribunt, sed tamen, quia ita ipsis placet, tribuunt; atque ad eam mentem verba ejus minus accommodata paululum inflectunt, ἐπί pro ἐν positum nulla reddita ratione, affirmantes. Ille objicit, hoc sapientiae Apostolicae minus convenire. Cum enim ejusmodi doctrina sit admodum ardua, et a sensu communi abhorrens, et alibi non doceatur in Scriptura, consentaneum erat, ut saltem hoc uno in loco doceretur aperte, et verbis disertis, aut saltem iis, quae falso quidem, sed tamen pro disertis ab iis habentur qui a nobis in hac causa dissentiunt. Si saltem dixisset ἐν ᾧ, non fuisset opus recurrere ad enallagem praepositionis ἐπί positae pro ἐν, et minus fuisset ambigua vocum ἐν ᾧ significatio: multo enim rarius, quam ἐφ᾽ ᾧ, significant eo quod, quatenus &c. Cum ergo Apostolus consulto dicere maluerit ἐφ᾽ ᾧ quam ἐν ᾧ, ac, quantum fieri potuit, ab illis removerit, et pluribus interpositis separaverit nomen ἀνθρώπου; atque ita impediverit ne ad id tanquam antecedens relativum ᾧ referretur, cur sine necessitate, sine ratione, malumus eius verbis et verborum collocationi vim aliquam inferre, ut id dicere aliquomodo videantur quod ex eis colligi nequit, quam retenta verborum ἐφ᾽ ᾧ proprietate, et Apostolico commatum situ eam sententiam verborum eius admittere, quam in se veram esse nemo non Pelagianus negare potest? Sed quid, inquit, impediet, quominus Pelagius aut Socinus eadem ratione objicere possint; Si Scriptura docere voluisset, vel peccatum generatione propagari, vel Christum esse Mediatorem merito et satisfactione; id expressuram fuisse, vel exprimere debuisse verbis claris et perspicuis, cum res sit ardua, nec satis ad communem hominum sensum accommodata? Omnino nihil impediet quominus hoc possint objicere, si velint, Pelagii et Socini sequaces; Sed nihil impediet etiam, quominus objicientibus respondeamus, non id quod vult D. G. nostrum non esse, Deo loquendi rationes et modos praescribere: Hoc enim, cum Dei mens et sententia versatur in quaestione, sophisticum videri possit; Sed quod res est, id neque a sensu conscientiae ullo modo abhorrere, et tam disertis ac claris verbis in Scriptura exprimi, ut, nisi iis magna vis afferatur, in alium sensum detorqueri nequeant.
